people.name: Fabian
people.summary: Bishop of Rome 236-250, chosen, Eusebius says, when a dove settled on his head although he was a layman. He organised Rome into seven ecclesiastical regions under deacons, brought back the bodies of Pontian and Hippolytus from Sardinia, and was martyred on 20 January 250 at the start of the Decian persecution; his Greek epitaph is in the Crypt of the Popes.
people.death: executed in the Decian persecution, 20 January 250

people.name: Cornelius
people.summary: Elected bishop of Rome in March 251 after a 14-month vacancy, Cornelius favoured readmitting the lapsed after penance and was opposed by Novatian, whose rigorist party elected him antipope. His letter to Fabius of Antioch gives the size of the Roman clergy (46 presbyters, 7 deacons, 7 subdeacons, 42 acolytes, 52 exorcists, readers and doorkeepers) and over 1,500 widows and poor on its rolls. Exiled by Gallus to Centumcellae, he died there in June 253.

people.name: Stephen I
people.summary: Bishop of Rome 254-257, Stephen accepted baptisms performed by heretics and threatened to break communion with Cyprian and the Asian churches who rebaptised, appealing to his succession from Peter; Firmilian of Caesarea attacked his arrogance in a letter preserved in Cyprian's correspondence. He died on 2 August 257, later venerated, without good evidence, as a martyr.

people.name: Sixtus II
people.summary: A Greek elected bishop of Rome in 257, Sixtus restored communion with Carthage after the rebaptism quarrel; on 6 August 258, under Valerian's second rescript, he was arrested while preaching in the cemetery of Callixtus and beheaded with four deacons, followed by Lawrence on 10 August. Damasus' epigram commemorates the scene.
people.death: beheaded in the catacomb of Callixtus, 6 August 258

people.name: Miltiades
people.summary: African-born bishop of Rome from July 311 to January 314, Miltiades recovered church property confiscated in the persecution, received the Lateran palace from Constantine and presided over the council of October 313 that heard the Donatist case in Fausta's house; he died on 10 or 11 January 314 before Arles met.

people.name: Julius I
people.summary: Bishop of Rome 337-352, Julius sheltered Athanasius and Marcellus of Ancyra, acquitted them at a Roman synod (340/341) and rebuked the eastern bishops for acting without Rome; Serdica's canons (343) gave the Roman bishop an appellate role. The Liber Pontificalis credits him with several churches, including the titulus Iulii in Trastevere traditionally identified with Santa Maria in Trastevere.

people.name: Liberius
people.summary: Bishop of Rome from 352, Liberius refused to condemn Athanasius at Milan in 355 and was carried off to Beroea in Thrace; after two years, broken by exile, he signed a compromise formula at Sirmium and returned in 358 to a Rome where the deacon Felix had been installed as rival, provoking riots. His reputation for lapsing made him the only early pope not venerated in the west. He died on 24 September 366, precipitating the Damasus-Ursinus clash.

people.name: Hippolytus
people.summary: Greek-writing presbyter and theologian at Rome, Hippolytus attacked Bishop Callistus for laxity and modalism and was set up as rival bishop by his followers, the first antipope; his works include the Refutation of All Heresies, a Commentary on Daniel and a Chronicle, and the Apostolic Tradition is attributed to him. A seated statue found in 1551 lists his works and an Easter table. Exiled with Pontian to Sardinia in 235, he died there and was reconciled as a martyr.

people.name: Dionysius of Alexandria
people.fullName: Dionysius the Great, bishop of Alexandria
people.summary: Pupil of Origen, head of the catechetical school and bishop of Alexandria from 247/8, Dionysius survived the Decian and Valerian persecutions in hiding and exile at Kephro in Libya, and his letters preserved by Eusebius are the main eyewitness source for the Alexandrian pogrom, the plague, the civil war of 261-262 and the rebaptism dispute. His stylistic argument that Revelation was not by the author of John's Gospel is a landmark of ancient literary criticism.

people.name: Julius Africanus
people.summary: Christian scholar from Aelia Capitolina who served under Severus at Edessa and built a library in the Pantheon for Severus Alexander. His Chronographiai in five books synchronised biblical and pagan history from creation to 221, setting the birth of Christ in the year 5500 of the world, and his Kestoi was a miscellany of magic, medicine and military lore. His letter to Origen doubting the authenticity of Susanna survives.

people.name: Caecilian
people.summary: Archdeacon and then bishop of Carthage (c. 311/312), Caecilian had opposed the cult of unauthorised martyrs and was consecrated by bishops accused of handing over scriptures; the Numidian episcopate rejected him, beginning the Donatist schism. Constantine, the Council of Rome (313), Arles (314) and the emperor in person (316) upheld him, and he attended Nicaea in 325.

people.name: Peter of Alexandria
people.summary: Bishop of Alexandria from 300, Peter fled during the Great Persecution, issued moderate canons on the readmission of the lapsed (306) and clashed with Melitius of Lycopolis, whom he excommunicated. Returning in 311, he was beheaded on Maximinus Daia's orders on 25 November 311, venerated by the Copts as the "seal of the martyrs".

people.name: Lucian of Antioch
people.summary: Presbyter and biblical scholar at Antioch, possibly a pupil of Paul of Samosata, whose revision of the Septuagint ("Lucianic recension") and New Testament text became standard in Syria and Constantinople. His pupils, the "Collucianists", included Arius, Eusebius of Nicomedia, Maris of Chalcedon and Theognis of Nicaea, so that later writers saw him as the root of Arianism. He was martyred at Nicomedia on 7 January 312.

people.name: Melitius of Lycopolis
people.summary: Bishop of Lycopolis in the Thebaid who during the Great Persecution ordained clergy in sees whose bishops were in prison or hiding and took a rigorist line on the lapsed, founding the schismatic "Church of the Martyrs". Nicaea allowed his clergy to keep their rank subordinate to Alexander's; his followers later joined the anti-Athanasian coalition, providing the charges at Tyre in 335.

people.name: Alexander of Alexandria
people.summary: Bishop of Alexandria from 312/313, Alexander condemned his presbyter Arius at a synod of about 100 bishops (c. 318-321) and circulated encyclicals against him; he led the anti-Arian side at Nicaea with his deacon and secretary Athanasius, whom he designated as successor before his death on 17 April 328.

people.name: Antony the Great
people.summary: Egyptian Christian from Coma in Middle Egypt who, after hearing the Gospel read c. 270, gave away his land and withdrew first to the edge of his village, then to tombs, then to a deserted fort at Pispir (c. 285) and finally to the Inner Mountain near the Red Sea (c. 313). Visited by crowds, he twice came to Alexandria (311 to encourage martyrs; 338 against the Arians) and corresponded with Constantine. He died in 356 aged about 105; Athanasius' Life of Antony made him the archetype of the monk across east and west.
people.death: natural causes on the Inner Mountain, 17 January 356 (trad.)

sources.w: Life of Paul the First Hermit

people.name: Pachomius
people.summary: Born to pagan parents in the Thebaid, Pachomius was conscripted c. 312 and converted after Christians fed the recruits; after baptism and training with the hermit Palamon he founded the koinonia at Tabennesi (c. 323), creating cenobitic monasticism: walled communities under a written Rule, with houses grouped by craft, daily work, fixed prayer and obedience to superiors. At his death in the plague of 9 May 346 the federation numbered nine male monasteries and two convents.

people.name: Hilarion
people.summary: Founder of Palestinian monasticism according to Jerome's Life, Hilarion was born at Thabatha near Gaza, studied at Alexandria, visited Antony, and lived as a hermit near Gaza from about 306; fleeing fame and persecution under Julian, he travelled to Egypt, Sicily, Dalmatia and finally Cyprus, where he died.

people.name: Evagrius Ponticus
people.summary: Born at Ibora in Pontus, ordained lector by Basil and deacon by Gregory of Nazianzus, Evagrius left Constantinople after a dangerous attachment to a married woman, stayed with Melania and Rufinus in Jerusalem and from 383 lived as a monk in Nitria and the Kellia. His Praktikos, Gnostic Chapters and On Prayer systematised desert spirituality, including the eight logismoi; condemned as an Origenist in 553, his works survived partly under others' names and in Syriac.

people.name: Melania the Elder
people.summary: Daughter of a consular Spanish-Roman family, widowed at 22, Melania left her son in Rome and went to Egypt (372), supporting the Nitrian monks exiled by Valens, then founded a convent on the Mount of Olives (c. 378-380) with Rufinus of Aquileia. Returning to Italy in 399, she inspired her granddaughter Melania the Younger; she died in Jerusalem c. 410.

people.name: Rufinus of Aquileia
people.summary: Monk, translator and historian from Concordia, Rufinus studied in Rome with Jerome, spent years among the Egyptian monks and founded a monastery on the Mount of Olives (c. 380). His Latin translations of Origen's De Principiis and Eusebius' Ecclesiastical History, which he continued to 395 with two new books, shaped western knowledge of Greek theology; the Origenist controversy turned Jerome into his bitter enemy.

people.name: Macrina the Younger
people.summary: Eldest child of a wealthy Christian family of Pontus, Macrina turned the family estate at Annesi into an ascetic community of women and men including her mother, and is credited by her brother Gregory of Nyssa with converting Basil to the ascetic life; Gregory's Life of Macrina and Dialogue on the Soul and Resurrection portray her as a philosopher.

people.name: Basil of Caesarea
people.summary: Cappadocian aristocrat educated at Caesarea, Constantinople and Athens (with Gregory of Nazianzus and the future emperor Julian), Basil turned to asceticism, writing the monastic Rules, and became bishop of Caesarea in 370. He built the Basileias charitable complex, resisted Valens' Homoian policy, and in On the Holy Spirit and Against Eunomius developed the formula of one ousia in three hypostases that triumphed at Constantinople in 381. His Address to Young Men defended reading pagan literature.

people.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
people.summary: Son of the bishop of Nazianzus, friend of Basil from student days in Athens, Gregory was a reluctant bishop of Sasima, then led the small Nicene community of Constantinople from 379, preaching the Theological Orations in the Anastasia. Installed in the Holy Apostles by Theodosius (380) and confirmed as bishop at the council of 381, he resigned amid quarrels over his translation from Sasima and retired to write poetry, including a long autobiographical poem.

people.name: Hilary of Poitiers
people.summary: Convert from a pagan family and bishop of Poitiers from c. 350, Hilary was exiled to Phrygia in 356 after the synod of Béziers; there he wrote De Trinitate and De Synodis, interpreting eastern theology for Latins, and addressed bitter invectives to Constantius. Returning c. 360, he led the restoration of Nicene orthodoxy in Gaul, sponsored Martin of Tours, and wrote some of the earliest Latin hymns.

people.name: Martin of Tours
people.summary: Son of a tribune from Savaria in Pannonia, Martin served in the guard cavalry (famously cutting his cloak for a beggar at Amiens) and left the army before a battle in 356 saying he was a soldier of Christ. A disciple of Hilary, he founded the monastery of Ligugé (c. 361), became bishop of Tours (371/2) and founded Marmoutier, destroying rural temples and sacred trees. He opposed the execution of Priscillian. Sulpicius Severus' Life made him the patron saint of Gaul and the Franks.

people.name: Cyril of Jerusalem
people.summary: Bishop of Jerusalem from c. 350, Cyril delivered the Catecheses (Catechetical Lectures), the fullest record of fourth-century baptismal instruction, preached in the Holy Sepulchre. He reported the cross of light of 351 to Constantius and was exiled three times by his metropolitan Acacius of Caesarea and by Valens, before attending the council of 381 as an accepted Nicene.

people.name: George of Cappadocia
people.summary: A former army contractor (Ammianus calls him born in a fuller's shop at Epiphania in Cilicia), George was installed as bishop of Alexandria in place of Athanasius in 357; he denounced citizens to Constantius, imposed taxes and attacked temples, and was lynched by the mob on 24 December 361. Julian demanded his large library, rich in philosophy, for himself.

people.name: Gregory of Cappadocia
people.summary: Imposed as bishop of Alexandria by a synod at Antioch and installed by the prefect Philagrius in March 339 during Athanasius' second exile, Gregory held the see amid violence until his death in June 345, which opened the way for Athanasius' return in 346.

people.name: Marcellus of Ancyra
people.summary: A champion of Nicaea, Marcellus taught that the Son and Spirit were extensions of the single divine monad that would return into God at the end, provoking the clause "of whose kingdom there shall be no end" in later creeds. Deposed in 336, defended by Julius of Rome and Serdica, he was a liability to Athanasius; his pupil Photinus went further.

people.name: Photinus
people.summary: Pupil of Marcellus and bishop of Sirmium, Photinus taught that Christ was a man born of Mary who became Son of God by adoption, a doctrine condemned by east and west alike; deposed at Sirmium in 351, he was briefly recalled by Julian, who praised him in a letter, and died in exile in Galatia in 376.

people.name: Basil of Ancyra
people.summary: A physician turned bishop of Ancyra (336), Basil led the homoiousian ("like in essence") party in the 350s, influential with Constantius until the Homoians Valens and Ursacius outmanoeuvred him at Rimini and Seleucia; he was deposed and exiled to Illyricum at the council of Constantinople in 360.

people.name: Aetius
people.summary: A former goldsmith and doctor turned dialectician, Aetius taught that the Son is "unlike" (anomoios) the Father in essence, since the unbegotten and begotten cannot share an essence; his Syntagmation survives in Epiphanius. Exiled by Constantius at Basil of Ancyra's urging, he was patronised by Gallus and Julian, and his disciple Eunomius gave the Anomoeans their name.

people.name: Eudoxius
people.summary: Leading Homoian prelate, successively bishop of Germanicia, Antioch (358) and Constantinople (360-370), Eudoxius dedicated the first Hagia Sophia and baptised Valens; famous for a flippant sermon beginning "the Father is impious, the Son pious", he was the chief architect of the Homoian church of the 360s.

people.name: Eusebius of Vercelli
people.summary: A Sardinian lector of Rome who became bishop of Vercelli (c. 345), Eusebius was the first western bishop to live communally with his clergy. Refusing to condemn Athanasius at Milan in 355, he was exiled to Scythopolis, Cappadocia and the Thebaid, joined the Council of Alexandria of 362 and, back in Italy, combated Homoianism with Hilary. The Codex Vercellensis of the Old Latin Gospels is traditionally his.

people.name: Lucifer of Cagliari
people.summary: Bishop of Caralis in Sardinia, exiled after Milan (355), Lucifer addressed to Constantius pamphlets of unprecedented violence (De non parcendo in Deum delinquentibus, Moriundum esse pro Dei Filio). Refusing the reconciliation of Alexandria (362), he consecrated Paulinus as bishop at Antioch, deepening its schism, and his followers, the Luciferians, formed a rigorist sect.
